content: Experimental studies have demonstrated that the severity of inflammation in the subarachnoid space is closely linked to the outcomes of bacterial meningitis. Corticosteroids are known to mitigate this inflammatory response. The objective of this analysis was to evaluate the impact of adjunctive corticosteroid therapy compared to placebo on mortality, hearing loss, and neurological complications in individuals of all ages diagnosed with acute bacterial meningitis. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, CINAHL, and LILACS, covering studies up to early 2015. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating the use of corticosteroids in acute bacterial meningitis. The methodological quality of the RCTs was assessed, and data on outcomes and adverse effects were collected. Subgroup analyses were performed based on age groups (children vs. adults), causative organisms, economic status of the study setting (low-income vs. high-income countries), timing of corticosteroid administration, and study quality. A total of 25 studies involving 4,121 participants (2,511 children, 1,517 adults, and 93 individuals from mixed populations) were included. Four studies were classified as high quality with no risk of bias, 14 as medium quality, and seven as low quality, resulting in a moderate overall risk of bias. Nine studies were conducted in low-income countries, while 16 were from high-income countries. The analysis revealed insufficient evidence to conclude that corticosteroids significantly reduced overall mortality (17.8% in the corticosteroid group vs. 19.9% in the placebo group; risk ratio [RR] 0.90, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.80 to 1.01; P = 0.07). Similarly, no significant reduction in mortality was observed in adults (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.05; P = 0.09). However, corticosteroids were associated with a reduction in severe hearing loss (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.88), any degree of hearing loss (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.87), and neurological sequelae (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.00). Subgroup analyses based on causative organisms showed that corticosteroids reduced mortality in cases of Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.98), but not in meningitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae or Neisseria meningitidis. In children with Haemophilus influenzae meningitis, corticosteroids significantly reduced severe hearing loss (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.59), but this benefit was not observed in meningitis caused by non-Haemophilus species. In high-income countries, corticosteroids were effective in reducing severe hearing loss (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.73), any hearing loss (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.73), and short-term neurological sequelae (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.85). However, no beneficial effects of corticosteroid therapy were observed in low-income countries. Subgroup analysis based on study quality revealed no significant effect of corticosteroids on severe hearing loss in high-quality studies. Corticosteroid treatment was associated with an increased risk of recurrent fever (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.47), but no other adverse events were significantly linked to its use. In conclusion, corticosteroids significantly reduced hearing loss and neurological sequelae in patients with bacterial meningitis, particularly in high-income countries. However, they did not reduce overall mortality. The data support the use of corticosteroids in bacterial meningitis patients in high-income settings, while no clear benefit was observed in low-income countries.
